text: In information theory, what does a low perplexity indicate?
options: The model is good at predicting the sample
The model has few parameters to train
The training data was collected recently
The model runs slowly at inference time
answer: The model is good at predicting the sample
explanation: It measures how well a probability distribution predicts a sample, and lower means better. The intuitive version is that perplexity is roughly how many options the model feels it has at each step, so 2 means it is usually confident between two choices.

text: A model is overfitting when it does what?
options: Has too few parameters to learn the pattern
Fits the training data too closely to generalise
Runs out of memory during training
Produces the same output for every input
answer: Fits the training data too closely to generalise
explanation: It corresponds too closely to one particular set of data and then fails on anything new, and an overfitted model has more parameters than the data can justify. Every regularisation technique, dropout included, exists to stop this, and large language models are trained in a regime where it is deliberately taken to the extreme.

text: Gradient descent is what kind of method?
options: A stochastic sampling algorithm
A method for compressing model weights
An iterative optimisation method for differentiable functions
A procedure for splitting a dataset into batches
answer: An iterative optimisation method for differentiable functions
explanation: A first order iterative algorithm for minimising a differentiable function, which means it follows the slope downhill in small steps. The batch size and learning rate are the two hyperparameters everyone tunes first, and the reason the loss curve is noisy rather than smooth is that each step uses a different sample of the data.

text: Dropout is a technique for reducing what problem in neural networks?
options: Vanishing gradients
Class imbalance
Slow convergence
Overfitting
answer: Overfitting
explanation: Overfitting, by randomly zeroing inputs and outputs during training so neurons cannot co-adapt to each other. It is only applied while training and never at inference, which is the detail that trips people up when they first see it in code.

text: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters
The next token in the output sequence
The attention weights between two tokens
The size of the model's parameter count
answer: The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters
explanation: Gradient computation for the parameter updates, by working backwards through the network and applying the chain rule. It is the reason training is not guesswork, and the reason the transformer abandoned backpropagation through time, since the whole sequence is processed in one forward pass instead.

text: A latent space is best described as what?
options: A physical region where models are stored on disk
A space where similar items sit close together
A list of tokens the model has never seen
The gap between training and inference
answer: A space where similar items sit close together
explanation: An embedding space defined by a set of latent variables that emerge from how similar items resemble each other. The geometry is the point, because it is what makes nearest neighbour search, clustering and the whole idea of interpolating between two images work.

text: Zero-shot learning is a setup where the learner sees what during training?
options: Only unlabelled images of the target classes
One labelled example of every class
No examples at all of the test time classes
Labels provided only at test time
answer: No examples at all of the test time classes
explanation: Nothing of the kind, and at test time it has to predict a class it has never seen, which is the name. It is a play on one-shot learning from computer vision, and it is the mechanism behind a large share of what people call a language model doing a task nobody trained it on.

text: What does the ReLU activation function do?
options: Squashes its input between zero and one
Halves its input when it is negative
Converts its input to a probability
Outputs the non negative part of its input
answer: Outputs the non negative part of its input
explanation: It is the ramp function, zero below zero and linear above, and being non linear is what lets a network of them solve non trivial problems. It replaced the sigmoid in hidden layers because it does not saturate on the positive side and it is far cheaper to compute.

text: What does the softmax function convert a tuple of numbers into?
options: A probability distribution over the possible outcomes
A single averaged value
A sorted list in descending order
A gradient for each input weight
answer: A probability distribution over the possible outcomes
explanation: A probability distribution over K outcomes, and it is almost always the last activation function in a classifier or language model. It is a generalisation of the logistic function to multiple dimensions, which is why you see the same function doing both binary and 50,000 way classification.

text: What is an epoch in neural network training?
options: One batch of data processed by the model
One full pass through the entire training dataset
One full pass of the loss function over the weights
One forward pass through a single layer
answer: One full pass through the entire training dataset
explanation: A full pass over the training data, after which the batch count resets. People say one epoch on a frontier model almost in the abstract, because the dataset is so large that nobody sees a second one, which is a good way to notice that the word is doing less work than people assume.

source.label: The PyTorch documentation on training loops

text: What is a token in a large language model?
options: A password that unlocks model access
A unit of text the model processes
A score that rates output quality
A file that stores model weights
answer: A unit of text the model processes
explanation: Models process numbers rather than text, so a tokenizer converts text into integer indices from a fixed vocabulary, often splitting words into subword pieces. The password reading is the common confusion because API keys are also called tokens, but a model token is a unit of text like part of a word.

text: What is limited by a language model context window?
options: The languages it can translate
The time its training takes
The users it can serve at once
The text it can consider at once
answer: The text it can consider at once
explanation: The attention mechanism only relates tokens within the context window, so anything beyond that limit cannot influence the output and must be truncated or retrieved another way. The language distractor plays on the word context, but the window is about how much text fits, measured in tokens, not how many languages are covered.

text: What is a hallucination in artificial intelligence?
options: A confident but false model output
A bug that crashes the program
A training run that diverges
An attack that steals model weights
answer: A confident but false model output
explanation: A hallucination is false or misleading information presented as fact, such as fabricated citations embedded in otherwise fluent text. The crash distractor misses the point: the program runs perfectly, which is exactly why hallucinations are dangerous in high-stakes uses.

text: What does the temperature setting control when generating text with a language model?
options: How fast the text is generated
How much memory the model uses
How random the word choices are
How many languages it supports
answer: How random the word choices are
explanation: Temperature scales the randomness of sampling: near zero the model almost always picks the top token and behaves deterministically, while higher values spread probability and produce more varied but riskier output. Speed is the natural confusion, but that is governed by hardware and serving, not by temperature.

text: What do neural scaling laws describe?
options: Shrinking chips from more transistors
Gains from scaling models and data
Decay from copying datasets repeatedly
Loss of signal in very deep networks
answer: Gains from scaling models and data
explanation: Neural scaling laws state that performance improves predictably as parameter count, dataset size and training compute grow, a relationship quantified by Kaplan and colleagues in 2020. The chip distractor is Moore's law, which is about transistors per chip, not about model loss falling with scale.

text: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
options: Linking several models in sequence
Training on human raters' thoughts
Repeating a prompt until it works
Getting step-by-step reasoning
answer: Getting step-by-step reasoning
explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting induces the model to work through intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, which Google researchers reported in 2022 improves multi-step and math performance, even zero-shot with phrase variants of let's think step by step. Linking models in sequence is a different idea, pipelines of models, not reasoning inside one response.

text: What is the core training objective of a GPT-style large language model?
options: Predicting the next token from prior tokens
Labeling each input image with bounding boxes
Scoring each reply with a learned reward model
Clustering input documents by shared topic labels
answer: Predicting the next token from prior tokens
explanation: Pretraining teaches the model the most likely next piece of text given everything before it. Reward scoring belongs to the later RLHF stage, not pretraining. That single objective at web scale is what produces few-shot abilities nobody explicitly programmed.

text: What makes text generation by most large language models autoregressive?
options: It samples all tokens in parallel in one step
It retrieves the answer verbatim from training data
It emits one token at a time conditioned on prior ones
It reranks completions with a separate reward signal
answer: It emits one token at a time conditioned on prior ones
explanation: Each new token joins the context for the next step, so output grows left to right. Parallel one-shot emission describes diffusion-style text models, not standard decoders. That is why generation cost grows with length and why KV caching matters.

text: What did the GPT-3 paper show about few-shot prompting?
options: It removes the need for any training data at all
It lets a model do tasks from examples in the prompt
It proves longer training always beats larger models
It guarantees cited answers from retrieved sources
answer: It lets a model do tasks from examples in the prompt
explanation: Brown and colleagues showed GPT-3 could perform unseen tasks when the prompt contained a few demonstrations and no weight updates. Zero-data learning is the stronger claim the paper never makes. That in-context ability, scaling with size, is what shocked the field in 2020.

text: What do query, key and value vectors do in attention?
options: They prune weak connections after training ends
They quantize weights for faster device inference
They label which data center served each request
They weight every token by relevance to each other one
answer: They weight every token by relevance to each other one
explanation: Queries score against keys and the resulting weights mix the values, so each position gathers context from the whole sequence. Quantization is the inference-speed distractor and touches weights, not token relevance. The scaled dot-product formula from 2017 is the version every transformer uses.

text: How does a vector database help a language model use stored knowledge?
options: By retrieving texts whose embeddings match the query
By retraining all model weights on each new document
By ranking candidate outputs with human preference scores
By compressing long prompts into fewer learned tokens
answer: By retrieving texts whose embeddings match the query
explanation: Documents are stored as embedding vectors and nearest-neighbor search returns the closest ones to the query embedding. Retraining on each document would be slow and destroy prior knowledge. That retrieval step is the R in RAG systems.

text: Which cost recurs every time a deployed model answers a query?
options: Dataset collection
Pretraining compute
Inference compute
Architecture design
answer: Inference compute
explanation: Training is paid once while each answer burns fresh inference compute on GPUs serving tokens. Pretraining is the big one-time bill people confuse with serving cost. That per-query cost is why distillation, quantization and efficient attention matter commercially.

text: When you use a chatbot day to day, does it learn from those conversations?
options: Yes, each conversation is added to its training data
Yes, but only for the account you are signed into
No, the trained model is the same for every user
Yes, once a conversation gets long enough
answer: No, the trained model is the same for every user
explanation: Training is finished long before you open the app: the model was pretrained on text and then tuned to follow instructions, and your messages do not change it. Feedback is the tempting wrong answer, because companies really do collect thumbs up and thumbs down, but that goes into a future release rather than into the model you are talking to. Fine-tuning is a real thing, but it is a deliberate project with its own training run, not something that happens because you were rude to a chatbot.
answerAliases: trained on a vast amount of text
pre-trained to predict the next word
fine-tuned to follow instructions and to behave as assistants

text: You want a chatbot to answer using documents that change every week. What is the usual fix?
options: Retrieval, which looks the documents up at question time
Fine-tuning, which retrains the model on the new documents
Prompting, which pastes the whole document set into every reply
Quantization, which shrinks the model so the documents fit
answer: Retrieval, which looks the documents up at question time
explanation: Retrieval leaves the model alone and looks the documents up each time a question arrives, so a file edited on Tuesday is live on Tuesday. Fine-tuning is the tempting wrong answer, and it is a genuine tool, but it is the right one for changing how a model behaves rather than for keeping a fact list current, because refreshing it means another training run. The term came from a 2020 paper that paired a model with an external store of documents it could consult on every question.
answerAliases: RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data
refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries

text: A lab publishes a model's weights so anyone can download them. What would open source additionally require?
options: That the weights be published at no charge
That the training data and code be public too
That the model run on hardware anyone can buy
That every model the lab has built be public
answer: That the training data and code be public too
explanation: Open source asks for more than the numbers: the training data, the source code, the evaluation results and the documentation as well. Free to download is the tempting wrong answer, because price and openness are different axes, and a model can sit on a public server under terms that forbid commercial use. The word licence is where the argument usually lands, since whether you may modify, fine-tune or redistribute released weights is set by the terms rather than by the download.
answerAliases: the model's source code, training data, evaluation results, intermediate checkpoints and technical documentation
permission to modify, fine-tune or redistribute it depends on its license

text: Chatbots often have standing instructions the user never sees. What are those called?
options: Hidden training data, added during pretraining
Model weights, rewritten for each new user
A secret API key the user must supply
System prompts, set by the app's maker
answer: System prompts, set by the app's maker
explanation: A system prompt is text the app maker puts in front of the model before your message, telling it who it is and what it should refuse. The training data answer is the tempting wrong one, because the weights were fixed months earlier and are not rewritten per user. It is also why the same underlying model can be a travel helper, a coding tutor and a customer support agent on the same day without anyone retraining it.

text: A chatbot seems to remember you between chats. Where is that actually kept?
options: In a notes file the app re-reads, not in the model
Inside the model's weights, which it rewrites as we talk
In the training set, which it adds each message to
In the model's context window, which grows with the chat
answer: In a notes file the app re-reads, not in the model
explanation: The model is unchanged, so whatever you told it last week lives in a notes file or summary the app keeps and pastes back in at the start of a conversation. The context window is the tempting wrong answer, but that is the current chat, and it empties when the chat ends, which is exactly why a new conversation starts blank. The layer that actually holds memory is the application wrapped around the model, the same layer that supplies its instructions and its tools.

text: Voice cloning lets you do which of these?
options: Hear a specific person say words they never recorded
Hear a recorded voice cleaned up and denoised
Hear one person's voice translated into another language
Hear a synthetic voice read a script in a neutral accent
answer: Hear a specific person say words they never recorded
explanation: It takes a sample of one person's voice and produces new sentences in it, including ones they never spoke. Ordinary text to speech is the tempting wrong answer, because that is what phone assistants have done for decades, and voice cloning is what makes the fake robocalls possible. The same technique is used to give a voice back to people who have lost their own, which is the one use nobody argues about.
answerAliases: generate speech that convincingly mimics specific individuals

text: When you describe a picture to an image generator, what is it actually doing?
options: Building a new image from scratch to match the description
Searching a photo library for a picture that already matches
Editing a stock photo to add the things you described
Printing the description as text onto a blank canvas
answer: Building a new image from scratch to match the description
explanation: Nothing is copied and nothing is searched for. The model has seen an enormous number of pictures with their captions and builds a new one out of what it learned, which is also why hands and written words so often come out wrong. The photo library idea is the most common misunderstanding, and it is the belief sitting behind most of the copyright fights. In 2022 the output of models like DALL-E 2 and Stable Diffusion was judged close enough to real photographs to be worth worrying about.
answerAliases: takes an input natural language prompt and produces an image matching that description
trained on massive amounts of image and text data scraped from the web

text: A chatbot asked about something it has never seen still gives a confident answer. Why?
options: It has no way to tell a confident guess from a real fact
It checks a live database and picks the closest match
It was ordered by its creators to never admit doubt
It copies the nearest sentence it memorised in training
answer: It has no way to tell a confident guess from a real fact
explanation: Predicting the next word means always producing something, and there is no separate step inside the model that checks whether the something is true, so a fluent wrong answer is indistinguishable from a right one. The database answer is the tempting wrong one, because retrieval genuinely exists, but it is a bolt-on and it is not where a model's own mistakes come from. Meta's Galactica shipped with the warning 'Outputs may be unreliable!' and was pulled two weeks after launch in November 2021.

text: A model is finished being pretrained. What does the next stage add?
options: Instruction following and human preferences
More raw text, so it knows more vocabulary
Faster hardware, so it answers in less time
A bigger context window, so it reads more at once
answer: Instruction following and human preferences
explanation: Once a model can predict text, the second stage teaches it to take instructions and to answer the way people prefer, which is what turns a base model into a chatbot. More raw text is the tempting wrong answer, because that is the first stage rather than the second. Hardware and context window are engineering choices rather than training stages, and both can change without the model being retrained at all.
answerAliases: fine-tuned to follow instructions and to behave as assistants
pre-trained to predict the next word

text: In plain English, what is an AI world model?
options: A simulator the AI uses to predict what happens next
A map of every country and city on the planet
A model of the weather, trained on past forecasts
A 3D video game engine that renders fake worlds
answer: A simulator the AI uses to predict what happens next
explanation: It builds a working simulation of a situation so it can try an action in its head and predict the result, rather than pushing a robot into the world to find out. A globe or a weather forecast is the tempting wrong answer, because a world model is built for one environment and is about cause and effect rather than geography. The idea is old, dating to the 1990s, and modern versions are used in robots, self-driving cars and interactive video.
answerAliases: builds an internal representation of an environment
predicts how that environment changes over time in response to actions
